Chapter 6: The Double Bind—Race, Religion, and the Limits of “American-ness”
Picture this: a young woman, standing in line at the DMV, waiting for her turn to renew her license. She’s lived in that city her whole life, but the questions never seem to stop. Someone asks about her accent, her name, even her headscarf. And then, the clerk looks up from her paperwork and says, “Where are you really from?”
That question sticks with her. It’s familiar, and honestly, it’s exhausting.
For a lot of people, being Muslim in America isn’t just about what you believe. It’s wrapped up in all these other things—your skin color, the language you speak at home, your family’s story—and how others see you, or think they see you.
No matter what, the idea of inclusion, of being accepted as “American,” always seems to come with some kind of filter. And that filter? It changes, depending on who’s looking.
Think about a high schooler, born and raised in the Midwest. One day, he’s asked to recite the Pledge of Allegiance a second time—just to “make sure.” His friends laugh it off, but he can’t help feeling singled out. It’s like no matter how much he tries, he’s always being tested, never quite passing.
This is the double bind so many live with: feeling like you’re not “American enough” in some places, not “Muslim enough” in others. It’s a constant balancing act.
Imagine a young professional in a big city. At work, she finds herself downplaying her faith, just to blend in. But at home, there’s a worry that she’s drifting away from her roots. The pressure to be both—and the fear of never being enough—is a quiet ache that doesn’t really go away.
Most people don’t notice this tension. They see the celebrations of diversity, the stories of “successful” Muslim Americans, and they figure, well, the hard part must be over. But if you’re living it, you know: those boundaries and rules about belonging? They’re always moving.
There’s a father who remembers a neighbor saying, “You speak English so well.” It was supposed to be a compliment. But really, it was a reminder—he’s always being measured against some invisible standard.
The truth is, the promise of belonging is always a little bit fragile, always comes with conditions. The lines between race, religion, and national identity blur together, and crossing them? That can come at a real cost.
For many, the dream of truly fitting in, of belonging, always seems just out of reach.
